<reason>A built a cleaner, more intuitive path: concrete cases (price-gouging, gambling apps, unreadable contracts) that track widely-shared moral intuitions, plus a sharp dilemma showing that B's "informed, voluntary, fraud/coercion-free" definition of consent smuggles in exactly the extra conditions the motion is about, meaning B's own opening effectively concedes that bare agreement isn't enough. The landlord pressure question was the debate's best moment: it forced B to construct an ad hoc "baseline entitlement/threat-offer" apparatus that, while internally coherent, visibly expanded mid-debate to patch each new counterexample — a pattern A explicitly and effectively named in the closing ("recruited for it"). B's threat/offer distinction and "exit collapses into voluntariness" move were genuinely strong philosophical resources and B never lost coherence, but B's central strategy — redefining "consent" until every hard case is defined away — is a harder sell against the plain reading of "consent alone," and B's repeated defense of the pharmacy case (transaction fine, injustice "upstream") never fully answered A's charge that this makes exploitation conceptually undetectable. B also suffered two clipped turns (opening and second rebuttal) versus A's one, an execution cost that lost potential force at key moments. On balance A controlled the framing, pressed the more damaging question, and closed more decisively.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's landlord pressure question (Turn 5) and B's baseline-entitlement answer (Turn 8), followed by A's closing charge that this apparatus was built reactively to survive each new counterexample — the exchange that best exposed whether B's standard was principled or ad hoc.</best_rebuttal>
